quotes.text: Erasure is best known for their fun, catchy, and upbeat synthpop hits. However, readers should know that as much as I do love that side of Erasure, my own personal tastes with the band run more toward their more mellow and contemplative songs.

While 'Rain' does have that classic 80's Erasure sound, here it feels vibrant and fun to me, full of sass and theatricality and with a knowing wink toward campiness that works, whereas on some of the other Cowboy songs that same indebtedness to their classic sound seems tired and somewhat formulaic.
One thing that Erasure has almost always been great at is opening their albums with excellent songs that are both great singles and/or songs that set the tone for the album.

'Sunday Girl' from 2007's Light At The End Of The World continues this fine tradition by walking the line between Erasure's classic pop sound and the current (for the time) club trends. Indeed, 'Sunday Girl' could have been a pop radio hit or a club favorite and been perfectly home in either place. This is the very skill Erasure made a career on in the 1980's and early 90's but they seemed to lose their way for a time and 'Sunday Girl' is vintage Erasure, only slightly updated.

Part of the success of The Innocents was, of course, the great songs on the album. However, The Innocents also received critical acclaim not usually given to synthpop groups because of the serious nature and issues dealt with at times on the album.

'Ship Of Fools' is a slower, more meditative number than the danceable singles the band was generally known for, and it showcases Andy Bell's superb vocal abilities and range, while Vince Clarke provides him a melancholic and sweeping bed of synth music that seems equal parts childhood whimsy and adult worry.
2005's Nightbird, a warm and lush album heavy on ballads and night songs, seemed a full return to form for the duo.
Clarke creates music with a groove that is both deep, yet soft, and lulls like a lullaby, while Bell sings a beautiful lyric about falling in love against your better judgment.

'Tenderest Moments' shines in the Union Street setting, with Andy Bell's vocals supported by Vince Clarke's acoustic guitar, some steel guitar touches, female backing vocals, and strings (and not a synth in sight), which gives 'Tenderest Moments' a fragile and delicate beauty that is perfect for the song and is sadly lacking from the original version.

While in the mid-90s the focus was still more on quantity and the quality noticeably declined, Andy Bell and Vince Clarke fortunately caught themselves again at the beginning of the 2000s and no longer demanded this high output from themselves.

The album 'Day-Glo (Based On A True Story)' is in fact a recycling of the leftover material from the quite fantastic album 'The Neon' (2020). Unfortunately, most of it is instrumental, which doesn't work for me in general. Some pieces sound like techno or house experiments, like on the concept album 'Ssss' by the project 'VCMG'. For me, the album is more of an electronic experiment and not a typical Erasure album.
To be quite honest, I have to say that most of the tracks sound like unfinished b‑sides of the last production to me. I think they wanted to forge the iron while it's still hot.

The album 'Cowboy' is, I think, pretty much the most average album by 'Erasure'. In contrast to the previous album 'Erasure', which almost made you fall asleep with its super long song lengths, here the tracks are produced in pleasant lengths suitable for radio. I have the feeling of an A/B test that Erasure has carried out here on a large scale.
Andy Bell has an innate warmth to his vocals that's never left him, and because the duo still sound so very Erasureish there's an instant nostalgic appeal to all of their stuff.
It's to Bell and partner Vince Clarke's credit then, that they've taken a less obvious and more satisfying route with Snow Globe.

The original songs are fairly subtle in their festive flavourings too; 'Bells Of Love' -thankfully not a yuletide reworking of 'Chains Of Love'- and the brilliant 'Make It Wonderful' are reassuringly Erasure-like, but they're not especially Christmassy; musically they're actually pretty sinister with Vince Clarke delivering dark, synthy-stabs, leaving Bell to pull them into pop shapes with his soaring voice.
Bell and Clarke never take the obvious route here. The song choices may be the most predictable possible but the arrangements are mental.
'Gaudete' is completely bonkers, a 16th century latin carol reborn as galloping electroclash. Bell's multi-tracked voice glides into a falsetto as Clarke navigates the odd medieval time signature.

The more traditional the song, the more Clarke wants to make it sound like christmas with the Cybermen. His arrangements are sparsely electronic, and as instrumentals bear basically no relationship to the familiar hymns. Instead they're chilly, embryonic electronica.

Snow Globe is one of the more palatable additions to the Christmas cannon, and a really good Erasure record to boot. It's not quite as dark or as bonkers as Kate Bush's Fifty Words For Snow, but it's a creative and welcome new soundtrack to the season of good will.
